title: Arrangement in Grey and Black No.1
altText: A woman in a black dress and white cap sits in profile, facing left, in a plain grey room. A framed picture and a curtain on the wall are arranged in calm, balanced shapes.

source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: An oil painting by James McNeill Whistler, an American artist, made in 1871. It is widely known as Whistler's Mother. The source page tags it Mothers, Family and Portraits. Whistler gave it a title that sounds like music, stressing the arrangement of colors and shapes.

descriptions.k: A woman sits very still on a chair. She wears black and a white cap. The wall is grey. Do you see a picture hanging behind her? How does the room feel: quiet or noisy?
descriptions.g12: James McNeill Whistler painted this quiet picture of a woman in a chair. He used mostly grey and black. She sits in side view, very still. The title sounds like music, not a person. Why might a painter use colors like a song?
descriptions.g35: James McNeill Whistler painted Arrangement in Grey and Black No.1 in 1871. Many people call it Whistler's Mother. A woman sits in side view in a plain room with a framed picture and a curtain. Whistler chose a title about colors, like a song. What do you notice about the shapes and colors, and how does the room feel?
descriptions.g68: In Arrangement in Grey and Black No.1 (1871), Whistler shows a seated woman in profile, in a plain room with a framed picture and a curtain. The title treats the painting like a musical arrangement of tones and shapes, not only a portrait. How do the straight lines of the room and the shape of the figure work together, and what mood do they create?
descriptions.g910: Whistler's Arrangement in Grey and Black No.1 (1871), popularly called Whistler's Mother, presents a seated figure in profile within a carefully balanced room of verticals and horizontals. By naming it like a musical piece, Whistler asked viewers to attend to tone and form. How does the tension between a family portrait and a formal study shape the emotion and meaning of the work?
descriptions.g1112: Arrangement in Grey and Black No.1 (1871), widely known as Whistler's Mother, shows how Whistler foregrounded design through a musical title, a limited palette, and a rigorous grid of verticals and horizontals. Viewers have read it as a tender family portrait, a formal experiment, or both. How do the title and composition negotiate between depicting a person and arranging tones, and what does each reading gain or lose?

k.daily: What is the woman doing in this picture? How do you know?
k.emotion: Does this picture feel calm, sad, or something else? Tell us what you see.
k.observation: Find the framed picture on the wall. What else do you find on the wall?
k.analysis: What shapes in the room are straight, and what shapes are curved?
k.line: Trace the line of her back and chair with your finger. Is it straight or bent?
k.shape: Which shapes look like boxes or rectangles in this picture?
k.color: The painter used lots of grey and black. How do those colors make you feel?
k.texture: Does her dress look soft or stiff? Tell us why.
k.space: Is she close to the wall or far from it? How can you tell?
k.light: Where is the light in this room? Where is it dim?
k.meaning: Why might a painter paint someone they love sitting quietly?
k.culture: Who in your family sits calmly like this? What do they do?
k.technique: The painter used oil paint. How could he make grey look smooth?
k.personal: If you painted a picture of someone in your family, what would you put behind them?
k.critical: What would you change about the wall to make the picture feel different?

g12.daily: What clues in the room and in the woman's pose tell you how she might be feeling?
g12.emotion: Describe the mood of the picture in two words. What shows that mood?
g12.observation: List everything you can find on the wall behind her.
g12.analysis: Why does your eye go to the dark figure first?
g12.line: Follow the straight lines of the wall, floor, and picture frame. What do you notice?
g12.shape: How do the rectangles in the room fit with the shape of the seated woman?
g12.color: How does the painter use only a few colors, and what feeling do they bring?
g12.texture: How can you tell her dress is a soft cloth even though the painting looks flat?
g12.space: How does the empty space in front of her feel?
g12.light: Where does the light fall in the room, and what does it show?
g12.meaning: Why might the painter pick a title about colors instead of a person's name?
g12.culture: What can this room tell us about how people lived long ago?
g12.technique: How did the painter show quiet with so few colors and shapes?
g12.personal: How would you pose a family member so they look calm and strong?
g12.critical: What would make the picture feel more cheerful if you added something?

g35.daily: Which details make Whistler's Arrangement in Grey and Black No.1 feel so still?
g35.emotion: How would you describe the feeling of this room, and which choices create it?
g35.observation: Look at the wall, curtain, and picture frame. What small details help fill the space?
g35.analysis: How does Whistler place the woman so that she seems balanced in the room?
g35.line: How do the straight lines of the room contrast with the shape of the figure?
g35.shape: How do the rectangles in the picture frame and wall compare with the curved shapes of the woman?
g35.color: How does the limited choice of grey and black affect the mood?
g35.texture: How does Whistler suggest different surfaces, like cloth, wall, and curtain, with similar colors?
g35.space: How does the large empty floor space affect the way you feel about the woman?
g35.light: How does soft light help create calm in the room?
g35.meaning: Whistler gave the painting a title like a piece of music. What might he want you to notice?
g35.culture: What might this painting tell you about family and home in the 1870s?
g35.technique: What might Whistler have done to blend greys and blacks into a smooth surface?
g35.personal: What would you want to tell the woman in the painting if you could talk to her?
g35.critical: Is this painting a portrait of a person, a design of shapes, or both? Use what you see to explain.

g68.daily: What does the stillness of the seated woman suggest about her character or the mood Whistler wanted?
g68.emotion: What emotions do the colors and pose create, and which details strengthen them?
g68.observation: Look at the wall again. Which element seems to frame or echo the figure?
g68.analysis: How does the balance between the figure and the surrounding rectangles organize the composition?
g68.line: How do the verticals and horizontals of the room contrast with the curves of the figure?
g68.shape: How does the repeated use of rectangles make the painting feel like a designed pattern?
g68.color: How does limiting the palette to greys and blacks change the way you read the scene?
g68.texture: How does Whistler create soft surfaces in the cloth and wall using tone rather than detail?
g68.space: How does the shallow room and profile pose affect the sense of space?
g68.light: How does gentle light shape the edges and mood of the figure?
g68.meaning: How does naming the painting like a musical arrangement change what viewers may focus on?
g68.culture: How does the formal pose reflect ideas about family and respect in the 1800s?
g68.technique: How might Whistler have worked to keep the greys harmonious across the whole canvas?
g68.personal: What would a portrait of someone you know look like if you treated it as an arrangement of shapes and colors?
g68.critical: Does the title help or limit your understanding of the painting? Defend your view.

g910.daily: How does the profile pose and rigid grid of the room shape your sense of the sitter's presence?
g910.emotion: What emotional tone does the painting set, and how much comes from its restraint?
g910.observation: Study how the picture frame, curtain, and figure relate. What does the arrangement imply about balance?
g910.analysis: How does the hierarchy of dark figure and lighter wall guide your reading of the composition?
g910.line: How do verticals and horizontals build a structure, and where does the figure interrupt it?
g910.shape: How do the rectangles and the seated silhouette create a rhythm across the canvas?
g910.color: How does the narrow range of greys and blacks create harmony, and what does it leave out?
g910.texture: What does the smooth handling of the surface reveal about Whistler's priorities?
g910.space: How does the flattened, shallow space reinforce the idea of a designed arrangement?
g910.light: How does the quiet, low-contrast light affect the emotional distance between viewer and sitter?
g910.meaning: Why might Whistler have used a musical title, and how does it shift attention away from a story?
g910.culture: How did the painting's later fame as an image of motherhood change how audiences view it?
g910.technique: How do the limited tones and flat shapes show Whistler's approach to oil painting?
g910.personal: How does your response change if you read the work as a tender family image rather than a formal study?
g910.critical: How would you evaluate whether an artist's title should guide how we interpret a painting?

g1112.daily: How does Whistler's insistence on a musical title complicate reading this painting as a straightforward portrait?
g1112.emotion: How does the austerity of palette and pose shape the emotional register, and could different viewers perceive it as solemn, tender, or severe?
g1112.observation: Examine the interplay of picture frame, curtain, and seated figure. Does the order feel balanced, confining, or both?
g1112.analysis: How does the composition use a rigid grid to organize attention and set the figure apart?
g1112.line: How do the dominant verticals and horizontals create tension with the softer contour of the figure?
g1112.shape: How does the repetition of rectangles function as a structural principle comparable to musical rhythm?
g1112.color: How does the restricted tonal scheme articulate Whistler's interest in harmony over description?
g1112.texture: How does the surface treatment reflect an emphasis on tone and design over narrative detail?
g1112.space: How does the shallow, planar space relate to later developments in modern art?
g1112.light: How does the muted lighting contribute to the painting's mood of withdrawal and calm?
g1112.meaning: What competing readings of the work, as portrait, symbol, or formal study, does the evidence support?
g1112.culture: How has the painting's afterlife as an icon of motherhood affected the way viewers see its original aims?
g1112.technique: How does Whistler's refined handling of oil paint reinforce his claim that painting can resemble music?
g1112.personal: How does your own experience of family shape your response to a painting that is both intimate and austere?
g1112.critical: What criteria would you use to decide whether the painting's fame depends on its subject or its design?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, medium and page tags (Mothers, Family, Portraits) read from the arthistoryproject.com page; no concerning terms. Only page text was read. Discrepancy: the page states the Louvre Abu Dhabi, but this painting (Whistler's Mother) is in the Musee d'Orsay, Paris, so that is used as the collection; it should be confirmed. The image itself was not visually inspected; a person should confirm it before release.

teacherNote.context: An 1871 oil painting by James McNeill Whistler, widely known as Whistler's Mother. The source page names the Louvre Abu Dhabi, but the painting is in the Musee d'Orsay, Paris.
directions: Ask students to sketch the painting using only rectangles and one curved shape to see its structure.
Discuss why an artist might title a portrait like a piece of music.
Have students photograph or draw a calm portrait of someone in a plain room and compare.
